content:
Game Levers in The One Ring: Playing in the Spirit of Tolkien In many roleplaying games, characters have access to very visible solutions.
In Dungeons & Dragons, they have spells, magic items, class abilities, miraculous healing, teleportation, fireballs, and a whole heroic toolkit built around solving problems through power.
In a science-fiction game, they might pull out a scanner, hack a door, repair a module, bypass an AI, or cobble together a drone.
But in The One Ring, the roleplaying game set in Tolkien’s Middle-earth, something changes radically.
The Player-heroes are usually neither wizards nor engineers nor superheroes. They do not carry a spectacular toolbox that allows them to mechanically neutralise every obstacle. And yet, they must survive, travel, investigate, persuade, fight, resist the Shadow, and sometimes change the course of a story far greater than themselves.
So what do they rely on?
The short answer would be: on what makes Tolkien feel like Tolkien.
Memory. Oaths. Ancient roads. Songs. Hospitality. Wisdom. Stealth. Courage. Pity. Alliances. Inner resilience. And, sometimes, the unexpected grace of the world.
These are the levers we need to learn how to bring to the table.
Do Not Look for a Substitute for Magic The first mistake would be to try to replace spectacular magic with something equally spectacular.
Just because a character cannot cast detect magic does not mean they need a disguised equivalent. Just because they cannot fly over a chasm does not mean you need to invent a gadget or a special power. Just because they cannot miraculously heal a wound does not mean healing should become trivial.
In The One Ring, the apparent lack of immediate solutions is not a flaw. It is the heart of the game.
The game itself is built around deeply Tolkienian situations: the Journey, Combat, and the Council. It also gives mechanical weight to the Shadow, the Eye of Mordor, magical treasures, and Patrons such as Bilbo or Gandalf. In other words, the system is not trying to emulate generic fantasy. It frames play around hardship, encounters, moral danger, and the crossing of a world heavy with history.
The real question is therefore not:
“What power can solve this problem?”
But rather:
“What does this problem reveal about the Player-heroes, the world, and the Shadow that is growing?”
1. Ancient Lore: Memory as a Tool for Action In Middle-earth, many solutions come from the past.
A forgotten name. A half-erased rune. A song handed down by the elders. A royal lineage. An abandoned road. A debt between two peoples. An ancient evil awakened beneath a hill.
Lore is a major resource because Tolkien’s world is layered. Nothing is merely there by accident. A ruin is not “a dungeon”. A forest is not “difficult terrain”. A sword is not “+1 damage”. Almost everything has an origin, a memory, a wound, or a lost nobility.
At the table, this can create powerful scenes.
The Player-heroes may recognise a Dwarven inscription. Remember an Elven song. Understand that a barrow is not just a hill. Identify the ancient name of a valley. Find, in a local legend, the clue that allows them to avoid a dangerous pass.
Ancient lore can replace utilitarian magic beautifully.
There is no need to cast a spell to “detect evil” if the Player-heroes know that this tower was raised by a fallen lord, that birds have avoided it for generations, and that the old folk refuse to speak its name after sunset.
That is not weaker. It is subtler.
2. Wisdom: Knowing When Not to Act In many games, a good solution is an effective action.
In The One Ring, a good solution can be restraint.
Do not take the treasure. Do not kill the defeated enemy. Do not enter the tomb. Do not answer the insult. Do not use the ancient object, even if it seems useful. Do not give in to fear, pride, or despair.
This is essential.
Tolkien’s world is not dangerous only because it contains Orcs, Trolls, and wraiths. It is dangerous because it tests the heart. The wrong decision is not always the one that fails immediately. Sometimes it is the one that succeeds too well, but at the cost of a compromise.
The Loremaster can therefore build scenes where temptation is more interesting than the obstacle itself.
An ancient blade could easily defeat a creature, but it is tied to a forgotten slaughter. A lord offers his help, but asks for betrayal in return. An Orc prisoner knows a secret path, but the Player-heroes must choose between brutal interrogation and a measure of pity. A treasure could save a starving village, but taking it would mean desecrating a tomb.
In this world, wisdom is a game lever because it protects the Player-heroes from the Shadow.
And sometimes, victory simply means remaining worthy.
3. Alliances: No One Saves the World Alone Middle-earth is a world of peoples, houses, lineages, and hospitality.
A company of Player-heroes should not solve everything alone, cut off from the rest of the world. Allies, hosts, guides, elders, village leaders, lords, craftsmen, Rangers, Elves, Dwarves, and Hobbits are all possible levers.
Help does not fall from the sky. It is earned, negotiated, and honoured.
This is where Councils become essential.
Convincing a Beorning chieftain to lend ponies. Receiving hospitality in an Elven house. Reminding a lord of an ancient oath. Seeking counsel from an old Ranger. Winning the trust of a suspicious community. Calling upon a debt earned during a previous adventure.
These scenes are not social filler between two fights. They are at the heart of the game.
In The One Ring, a good relationship may be worth more than a magical item.
A company that saved a village may later find shelter there. A respected Dwarf may open doors in a closed community. A kindly Hobbit may defuse a tension that a warrior would only worsen. A hero known for keeping their word may be believed where others would be rejected.
Reputation becomes a resource.
4. Roads, Places, and the Journey The Journey is not a transition. It is a trial.
That is a crucial difference from many roleplaying games, where travel mainly connects two important scenes. In The One Ring, the road is part of the story.
A mountain, a moor, a forest, a river, or an old road are not mere backdrops. They are forces. Memories. Dangers. Sometimes even allies.
An ancient Elven path may shield travellers from watchful eyes. A forest may mislead those who enter it with ill intent. A forgotten ford may save a company being hunted. An old spring may restore courage. A ruin may reveal a fragment of history. A mountain pass may force a choice: gain time, or protect the weakest.
For the Loremaster, this means that places should have personality.
Not necessarily consciousness. There is no need to make everything supernatural. But every important place should ask a question.
What remains here from the past? Who suffered here? Who still protects this place? What has the Shadow corrupted here? What can the Player-heroes learn here? What does this place demand of them?
Middle-earth is not a map to cross. It is a world that answers.
5. Songs, Names, and Tales In Tolkien, words matter.
Ancient names, songs, poems, genealogies, oaths, and tales are not mere literary ornaments. They grant access to the depth of the world.
At the table, they can become very concrete levers.
A song may give heart to a weary company. An ancient name may make a creature hesitate. A genealogy may legitimise a request before a lord. A poem may reveal the location of a door. A tale may remind a people of what they once were. An oath spoken publicly may transform a political scene.
But be careful: this does not mean turning songs into permanent mechanical bonuses or disguised spells.
A song is not a buff. A name is not a magic keyword. A tale is not a utility skill.
Their power comes from meaning.
They remind the Player-heroes that they are not merely trying to survive. They are taking part in a story greater than themselves.
6. Stealth and Humility Hobbits are probably the best lesson in Tolkienian game design.
They are not powerful. They are not impressive. They do not dominate through weapons, magic, or science. And yet, they are decisive.
Why?
Because they are quiet. Resilient. Faithful. Underestimated. Attached to simple things. Capable of pity. Capable of carrying on when they should never have made it this far.
In play, this means that the most interesting solutions are not always heroic in a spectacular sense.
Hiding in a cart. Taking a muddy path. Sharing a meal to ease suspicion. Listening instead of speaking. Fleeing rather than fighting. Lying clumsily, but bravely. Sparing a wretched enemy. Carrying an exhausted companion.
These are modest actions. But in Tolkien’s world, they can carry immense weight.
The Loremaster should therefore beware of a common bias: rewarding only clever, tactical, or impressive decisions.
In The One Ring, a humble decision may be the truest one.
7. Ancient Objects: Rare, Meaningful, Never Neutral There are indeed wondrous objects in Middle-earth.
Ancient blades. Elven ropes. Maps. Jewels. Rare herbs. Gifts offered by great figures. Dwarven relics. Artefacts inherited from an earlier age.
But they should never become a catalogue of magical equipment.
A good Tolkienian object is not merely useful. It has a history.
It comes from somewhere. It belonged to someone. It carries a memory. It may open doors, inspire respect, awaken greed, or draw the attention of the Shadow.
The danger, for the Loremaster, is to treat these objects as conventional mechanical rewards.
An ancient sword should not merely deal more damage. It may be recognised by an old enemy. It may impose a responsibility. It may be tied to a vanished lineage. It may give courage to those who know its name. It may also become a burden.
In The One Ring, owning something powerful is never trivial. Magical treasures exist, but they belong within a moral and narrative tension shaped by the Shadow and the Eye of Mordor.
8. Courage and Hope Tolkien’s heroes do not press on because they are certain they will win.
They press on because they must.
This is vital to convey in play. Courage is not the absence of fear. It is the ability to continue despite fear, exhaustion, rain, wounds, bad news, and the sense that all may already be lost.
In The One Ring, Hope and Shadow are not decorative concepts. They are central axes of play.
An interesting obstacle is therefore not only:
“How do you get past it?”
But also:
“What does it cost you to keep going?”
The Player-heroes may lose time. Vigour. Trust. Innocence. A relationship. A refuge. A good reputation. A part of themselves.
That cost is what gives success its weight.
A company that crosses a hostile land without losing a single Endurance point, but with its Hope worn thin, has lived through a truly Tolkienian adventure.
9. Pity as a Narrative Force Let us say it plainly: if your table leaves no room for pity, it will miss part of Tolkien’s heart.
Pity is not naivety. It is not weakness. It is not a refusal to play effectively.
It is a moral choice that can change the story.
Sparing an enemy. Listening to a miserable creature. Not finishing off a traitor. Giving a second chance to someone who does not truly deserve it. Recognising suffering even in an adversary.
In game terms, this is delicate, because pity must not become a profitable strategy every time. It should not be rewarded mechanically and automatically.
Sometimes it will cost dearly. Sometimes it will seem useless. Sometimes it will return much later, in an unexpected way.
But it must exist as a real possibility.
If every creature encountered is only an obstacle to eliminate, we fall back into a fantasy of tactical cleansing. That is not the same imaginary world.
10. Providence: Handle with Care In Tolkien, there is a form of meaningful chance. An unlikely meeting, unexpected help, a turn of events that seems to answer to something greater than the will of heroes and enemies alike.
In play, this is a powerful but dangerous tool.
Used poorly, it becomes a deus ex machina: the players fail, then the Loremaster rescues them. That is bad play.
Used well, it gives the sense that the world is larger than the will of the Player-heroes and their foes.
Rain washes away tracks. An animal briefly guides the travellers. An old ally appears at the right time, not because the scenario demands it, but because the Player-heroes had planted that possibility earlier. A dream offers an image, not a solution. An enemy hesitates because of a past act of mercy.
Providence works best when it responds to choices the players have already made.
It must not replace their decisions. It should give them resonance.
How to Prepare a Scene When preparing a situation for The One Ring, avoid thinking only in terms of obstacle and solution.
Try this checklist instead:
What ancient lore can illuminate the scene? A song, a rune, a legend, a forgotten name, a map, a witness.
What moral choice is at stake? Temptation, pity, pride, fear, loyalty, vengeance, oath.
What ally might help? A village, a host, a guide, a Patron, a debt, a reputation.
What place shapes the scene? Forest, ruin, river, tomb, ancient road, hill, house, threshold.
What price must be paid? Fatigue, delay, Shadow, loss of resources, debt, wound, separation.
What humble solution might work? Stealth, patience, hospitality, listening, flight, negotiation, sacrifice.
This checklist is often enough to turn a plain scene into a Tolkienian one.
A Few Examples A Bridge Has Collapsed Generic fantasy version: the characters cast a spell, quickly build a crossing, or find an item that lets them pass.
The One Ring version: they search for a forgotten ford mentioned in a local song, bargain with a suspicious ferryman, accept a long detour by an ancient road, or build a raft while losing precious time as the Shadow draws nearer.
The issue is not only crossing. The issue is: what does the detour cost, and who helps the Player-heroes?
A Wight Haunts a Ruin Generic fantasy version: fight the undead creature.
The One Ring version: the Player-heroes must learn its name, understand what wrong binds it there, restore an object, find a descendant, sing an ancient lament, or wait for dawn before crossing the threshold.
The issue is not only defeating it. The issue is: what memory asks to be laid to rest?
Orcs Block a Mountain Pass Generic fantasy version: tactical fight.
The One Ring version: the Player-heroes observe the rivalries between two bands, create a diversion, take a dangerous goat track, free prisoners who know another way, or abandon their baggage to save the weakest.
The issue is not only winning. The issue is: should they fight, bypass, sacrifice, or endure?
A Lord Refuses to Help Generic fantasy version: persuasion roll.
The One Ring version: the Player-heroes remind him of an ancient oath, present an heirloom, bring forward someone they once saved, accept a task in exchange, or confront him with the shame of his inaction.
The issue is not only convincing him. The issue is: what might awaken honour?
The Real Engine: Remaining Worthy as the World Darkens In the end, the levers of play in The One Ring do not replace magic or technology.
They shift the centre of gravity.
In another game, the question might often be:
“What means do we have to solve this problem?”
In The One Ring, the question becomes:
“What choices will we make, and what will they reveal about us?”
That is where the game becomes powerful.
The Player-heroes do not triumph because they have the best powers. They triumph because they remember, because they keep their word, because they inspire trust, because they know the roads, because they respect ancient places, because they know how to ask for help, because they refuse certain easy paths, because they carry on despite fear.
And sometimes, because they choose pity where everything pushed them toward violence.
These are the true levers at the table in Middle-earth:
memory, oaths, honour, songs, alliances, hospitality, ancient roads, objects heavy with history, stealth, endurance, Hope, pity — and the ability to resist the Shadow.
This is not a fantasy of power.
It is a fantasy of inner steadfastness.
And that is precisely what makes The One Ring a game apart.
title: Game Levers in The One Ring: Playing in the Spirit of Tolkien

Dour-Handed is a starting virtue common to all the culture.
It gives 2 bonuses
+1 damage to Heavy Blow +1 to feat die for each Pierce (combat special damage for swords, bows and spears) Pay attention that in the Alpha release of the pdf rule it was like that, the pierce bonus wasn’t present !
Warning :
This tutorial is compatible with Tor2e v2.0.7 and more.
Create the Virtue First step create the Dour-Handed virtue with value and description. No Active Effect yet. Wait for next steps.
Heavy Blow Damage Bonus To setup this bonus, you need to add an Active Effect to the virtue Dour-Handed.
First, open the Dour-Handed item, go to the Effects tab and click on ‘+’.
You are about to create a new AE for this Virtue.
Choose a label to explain what it is for, change the icon for an appropriate one.
Very Important !! Verify that the “Effect suspended” is unchecked and “Transfer Effect to Actor” is checked.
After this check, you have to go to Effects Tab. In this tab, you will add the dynamic part of the AE; What it has to do !
Click “+” :
choose from the Attribute Key list : Heavy Blow Damage Mode should be Add Effect Value 1 This video shows how to do it.
Pierce feat die bonus To setup this bonus, you need to add a new Active Effect to the virtue Dour-Handed. At this point, you should already have 1 AE. First, open the Dour-Handed item, go to the Effects tab and click on ‘+’.
You are about to create a second AE for this Virtue.
Choose a label to explain what it is for, change the icon for an appropriate one.
Very Important !! Verify that the “Effect suspended” is unchecked and “Transfer Effect to Actor” is checked.
After this check, you have to go to Effects Tab. In this tab, you will add the dynamic part of the AE; What it has to do !
Click “+” :
choose from the Attribute Key list : Pierce Mode should be Add Effect Value 1 This video shows how to do it.
Important For system development purpose, I don’t add +1 to feat die but instead I decrease the edge threshold to pass to trigger a Piercing Blow.
Conclusion To create a Dour-Handed virtue with full automation, you have to keep in mind that you need 3 steps :
Create a Virtue Add Heavy Blow bonus Add Pierce bonus Feel free to play around with the AE, it is a great opportunity of automation but keep in mind it is still a WIP feature of Foundry VTT.
title: Set up Dour-Handed with Active Effects

content:
A quick blog post today about a question I often see on discord, facebook, …
How do I setup weapon that can be used in one hand or two hands like longswords or spears.
The main problem is the difference between stats when you use the weapon with one hand or two hands. And the system doesn’t have any way to have different stats in the same weapon depending on how mane hands you use.
You have to find a workaround
Setting up the system to handle weapon usable both in one-hand and two-hands It is quite easy to setup TOR for one hand/two hands weapon like spears. you have to use 2 items (one for one hand and the other for two hands) and the trick is to change the load of one of the 2 items to 0 in the character sheet.
Note The best way is to change the load of the item in the sheet as Foundry VTT does copy of the item when you drop the item in a sheet so the original item is not updated. This way you always the right stat for the reference item and you only change the instance of the item in the sheet.
Conclusion To have a really neat and clean way to handle this feature in TOR would mean a lot of code and complexity, it would be over engineering to do it so I chose not to do so and use this workaround.
title: How to setup 1-hand and 2-hands weapons

content:
Lots of systems, having an item (magical or not) can modify the characteristics of a Hero or an Adversary. In Foundry VTT, it is possible to have this automation using Active Effect. In this article I will show you how to automate the modification of the Piercing Blow modification using a keen Weapon (Reward).
I will tell you how to do it, how it is working and also what is the limitation (TOR2e system).
Attacking with a standard simple weapon With this weapon, no active effect, you can see that the piercing blow threshold is 10 (which is the standard value). No modification at all whatsoever.
With a standard weapon equipped, the system will try to beat 10 on the feat die to trigger a piercing blow.
Attacking with a keen weapon A keen weapon (one of the reward available to player in the Core Rules), this weapon has a special capacity, it triggers a piercing blow on a 9+ (9, 10 and Gandalf Rune for Character and Sauron Eye for Adversary) instead of 10.
With a keen weapon equipped (a weapon with an active effect keen), the system will try to beat 9 on the feat die to trigger a piercing blow.
But … How to create such Active Effect in Tor2e ? (please read next paragraph).
How to create a keen Active Effect In the video below, you can see how to create such active effect but before, you have to know a few things about active effect and Foundry VTT.
Note First of all, you have to add the active effect on an item in the Item Sidebar, you can’t modify an active effect in an item embedded in an actor (actor is the FVTT term for characters, adversaries, npcs, …).
Secondly, please notice, active effect are not items you can drag’n drop on an item/actor, you need to add it using the active effect tab in an item sheet.
Add an active effect to the item So to add an active effect, you need to go to the sidebar and open the item sheet you want to modify, then you go to the active effect tab in the sheet. In the active effect tab, you have to click on the "+" on the sheet.
A customization popup appears on the screen to set up the active effect data. You will have to fill some of the fields to make it work !
Important To have an active effect active in your sheet, you need to uncheck the “Effect Suspended” checkbox. If you forget to uncheck this checkbox, that active effect will have NO EFFECT in your actor !
In fact, this checkbox is used by FVTT to know the effect should be suspended (so not active) or if it should be actve (this is what we want). This is mainly the source of error and mistake when you create your active effect, it is not working.
Often You forgot to modify the checkbox so it is doing nothing !
Create an effect in the Active Effect Once, the item has an active effect and this active effect is not suspended (so it is active), you need to create an effect. To do so, go to the Effects tab and add an effect using "+" icon. The effect has some data to specify (Attribute Key to modify, Method of modification and Value).
For our keen Active Effect purpose, you need to choose :
Attribute Key –> Weapon Piercing Blow Change Method –> Downgrade Value –> 9 Now if you test, you should have the expected result, triggering a piercing blow on 9. But if you look closely, you can see a little issue (see below for explanation).
Current Tor2e System limitations If you look at the video until the end, you will notice that if you have an item with a keen active effect, even if you don’t attack with the weapon, or you even don’t have the item equipped, the piercing blow threshold is downgrade to 9 which is wrong ! The system shouldn’t modify the piercing blow threshold.
I have a solution to do it correctly, but I haven’t coded it yet so … for now, you need to modify the sheet, deleting the item or keep in mind and compute the proper value of the threshold in your head.
Conclusion To create a keen Active Effect, you have to keep in mind [how to do it correctly](#keen-active-effec and to know some [limitations](#navigating-between-input-fields of the system.
Walking through the active system attribute key list, you notice there is some attribute you can change, I also will add new later on. You can play with all the attributes but keep in mind it is a WIP feature that will evolve and it is not perfect.
title: Active Effect for Piercing Blow

content:
Developing a system for a TTRPG is sometimes complicated because you have to make some choice because there are as many opinions as there are people playing :) And sometimes, opinions are opposite. So I try to make the system the less opinionated to let people use it and play as they want, but there are some limits.
For this first post, I will show you some keyboard keys you can use to ease your life. I have made a short video to show you how to do it, in the bottom of the video you will see the keyboard keys I use.
Navigating between input fields If you need to go from one input field to the next one, you can use the tab key as it is shown in the video below.
Tip Use Tab Key to go to next field and Shit+Tab to the previous one.
It is fairly simple and easy to use when you want to fill quickly the value of the input field. Please keep in mind, it is very valuable with the last tips of this post about modifying numeric values with arrow keys.
Skill value modification One of the most misunderstood feature of Tor2e, it’s how to modify the skill values (common skills, combat proficiencies, …). I think it is the majority of the question we had, it is about this feature !
- How the hell am I modifying the skill value in the sheet ?
- There is a bug, I can’t change the value of my sheet !
Well in fact, bugs can happen, I had experienced a lot, I am sorry about that, but it is part of the job of coding ;) But there is no bug with the modification of the skill value :
Tip You HAVE to use the Alt Key to add one (+1) to the skill value and as a contrary Shift + Alt Click to decrease one (-1) to the skill value.
You can have a look at the video below to see an example of “How to modify the skill values of a character sheet”.
Why did you do that It is quite simple, character sheet should not be modified by miss click or by error, so I needed to find a solution, this one seems to be the best for me and for my players. I should have made another decision … but you know … if it wasn’t the case, I won’t be here writing about that so … It is made this way and I tried to do so all over the sheets. So if you want to toggle a state (weary, miserable), you have to do the same.
Modifying numeric input fields Last tips of the post, but not the least, because I think the most unknown ! It is about modifying numeric value using arrow keys (up and down). For all numeric input field, you use up arrow to add 1 and down arrow to decrease 1 from the current value. It is very straight forward and very useful if you use it with the first tip about navigating between input fields.
Tip Use Up key to add 1 and Down key to decrease 1.
Please look at the video below to see an example of how to use that in the System.
Cherry on the Cake If you use the up and down key, you will notice that the value of the field is limited top and bottom with a value I have set up in the system. This way you won’t fill the input field with a wrong value. It is very convenient and avoid to type wrong value.
Even if you type a wrong value (not an integer for example), there is a tick and a cross to tell you if the value is “ok” or not for the system.
Conclusion I wanted for a while to share with 3 these 3 tips, because one is the most misunderstood and one is the most unknown :) I hope it will help you !
Use these 3 tips to easy your life using the system and have more times to enjoy and roleplay.
Take in this hard time and stay in touch for more news.
title: Keyboard Usage

content:
“Very best wishes for Yule - J. R. R. Tolkien” ― Tolkien to Richard Jeffery in Letter 347, (dated 17 December 1972)
How to start a blog on Tolkien’s Legacy in a better way than quoting J.R.R. Tolkien, himself ! In this period of holidays and end of year, called Yule in Middle-Earth, I decided to start a blog to share the little I know if it helps, a small gift to Tolkien’s work.
Just a few words about me, I am a Table Top Role Player since the 80s, I have 3 children and a Wife, and I am a professional developer. Saying that, I said nothing important but combining all together and thanks to the lockdown, last year I started as a hobby a project (it’s nearly the first anniversary of the project) to integrate “The One Ring” (v1) for Foundry VTT.
At first, it was the v1 of the TTRPG (now it is ended) then the v2 (The One Ring TTRPG) after the Kickstarter.
After nearly one year of coding, chatting with the community, role-playing with friends, I think it’s time to aggregate some of my experience somewhere. People often ask me the same questions about The One Ring or the System I have done for FVTT, so it will be the place to put all the answers, all the reflexions I have, ideas, …
Please take a sit, get some drink and meet me elsewhere on this blog to talk of Tolkien, Middle-Earth or TTRPG ;)
I wish you all the very best for Yule !
title: Very best wishes for Yule
